source_refs.note: Topic printed 1.1.1.1 Other Methodologies (Scrum and Lean) with Figs. 1.4 and 1.5 (PDF 13-15, printed 10-12). MCQ 5, short question 4 and long question 3 are answered.

blocks.text: Scrum is an Agile framework widely used for managing and completing complex software projects. It promotes iterative progress, collaboration and flexibility, so it suits dynamic environments where requirements change often. It is built around roles, events and artifacts that give a structured yet adaptable approach (Fig. 1.4).

items: Roles: the Product Owner defines the product backlog and keeps the team on the highest-priority items; the Scrum Master facilitates the process, removes obstacles and makes sure the team follows Scrum; the cross-functional Development Team delivers the product increments.
Events: sprints (time-boxed iterations), sprint planning, daily stand-ups, sprint reviews and sprint retrospectives.
Artifacts: the product backlog (prioritized list of features and requirements), the sprint backlog (tasks for one sprint) and the increment (the working product at the end of the sprint).

blocks.text: Scrum suits projects with frequent updates and evolving requirements, such as mobile applications and web development, where quick adjustments follow user feedback and market changes. It may not suit projects with well-defined requirements and little expected change, such as embedded systems with hardware integration and strict regulations, or safety-critical software such as medical or aerospace systems that need thorough documentation and extensive validation.

Lean software development is an iterative approach that emphasizes efficiency, eliminating waste and delivering high-quality products quickly. Derived from Lean manufacturing principles, it delivers value to the customer by optimizing the flow of work and minimizing unnecessary activities (Fig. 1.5).

items: Eliminate waste: remove activities that add no value for the customer.
Amplify learning: build continuous improvement and learning.
Decide as late as possible: decide with the latest information to reduce uncertainty.
Deliver as fast as possible: deliver small increments of features quickly.
Empower the team: give teams the authority and responsibility to decide and solve problems.
Build integrity in: keep quality throughout development.
See the whole: consider the entire system and its context to optimize the flow of work.

blocks.text: Lean suits projects needing rapid delivery and frequent iterations, such as startup software, mobile applications and web-based services: a startup building a new mobile app benefits by iterating quickly on user feedback. It may not suit projects that need extensive upfront planning and are highly complex or regulated, such as large enterprise systems, embedded systems or safety-critical applications like aviation control software, which demand rigorous documentation, testing and compliance.

blocks.alt: Top: the Scrum lifecycle from product backlog through sprint planning, sprint backlog and the sprint with its daily scrum to the increment and sprint review, with the retrospective feeding back to planning. Bottom left: the seven Lean principles as a numbered list. Bottom right: two linked loops for Dev and Ops with plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate and monitor.
blocks.caption: Scrum, Lean and DevOps (original diagram after Figures 1.4 to 1.6).
blocks.long_description: In Scrum the product owner keeps a prioritized product backlog; at sprint planning the team takes items into a sprint backlog, works on them in a sprint of a few weeks with a short daily scrum, and produces a working increment that is shown at the sprint review; a retrospective then improves the next sprint. Lean lists seven principles: eliminate waste, amplify learning, decide as late as possible, deliver as fast as possible, empower the team, build integrity in and see the whole. DevOps joins development and operations in one continuous loop of planning, coding, building, testing, releasing, deploying, operating and monitoring.

blocks.prompt: Which role removes obstacles and facilitates Scrum practices (MCQ 5)? Identify the key components of Scrum and how each helps project management (short question 4).
blocks.explanation: The Scrum Master, option (b). Roles give clear responsibility (Product Owner sets priorities, Scrum Master keeps the process running, the team builds); events give a regular rhythm of planning, daily coordination, review and improvement; artifacts make the work visible (what is wanted, what is in this sprint, what has been delivered).

blocks.prompt: A project needs extensive documentation and has strict regulatory requirements. Why might Scrum not suit it, and what could be used instead (long question 3)?
blocks.explanation: Scrum changes requirements sprint by sprint and keeps documentation light, while regulated projects need fixed, fully documented requirements and formal approval at each stage; a plan-driven model such as the Waterfall model, with complete documentation and sign-off before each phase, fits better.

items: Scrum: Agile framework with roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Development Team), events (sprints, planning, stand-ups, review, retrospective) and artifacts (product backlog, sprint backlog, increment); suits mobile and web apps, not embedded or safety-critical systems.
Lean: from Lean manufacturing; seven principles from eliminating waste to seeing the whole; suits startups and fast-iterating apps, not heavily regulated systems.
